I notice that the west of the U.S. has more hot all-time records than the rest of the country and that the middle of the U.S. has more cold. I also noticed that there are significant temperature spikes from 1991 to 2021.

I wonder why the west coast specifically is warmer, and why the east coast doesn't really have much going on. I'm also curious how this relates to other countries? Is this an average around the world? Is this drastically different from other places?

This relates to my community because we'll eventually have to adapt to changing temperatures. Although where I'm located doesn't have drastic temperatures, I'm sure the overall effect on the country will affect me as well.

A catchy headline idea could be "Temperature extremes in the U.S."

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:

- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

raw_comment:
I noticed that the majority of all time records for heat were set in the West Coast, whereas the majority of all time records for cold were set in the middle of the United States. Additionally, I noticed that heat broke the majority of all-time temperature records at weather stations.

I wonder how the temperature records set in the United States correlates to temperature records set around the world. Which months are the most popular for all-time temperature records for heat and cold? Which states hold the record for the highest and lowest temperatures? 

This relates to me and my community because all-time temperatures will eventually force us to make adaptations to our lives. For example, Texans experienced a cold storm that left them without power, water, and food for days.

This graph depicts the percentage of weather stations that broke all-time temperature records and where they were set in 2021. A catchy headline I came up with was “Falling and Rising All-Time Temperatures Are Surprising.”

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

raw_comment: The temperature records established in 2021 are shown in this graph. It also displays the annual temperature records from 1991 through 2020. In June of 2021, the northwest faced an intense heatwave. I believe the wildfires that raged across the West had an impact on these figures. The Midwest has been hit by a severe cold spell. I'm curious as to how the environment and temperature will change in the next years. If the temperatures continue to rise, there will be a slew of issues, and I'm not sure what they will be. I also noted that Hawaii experienced a cold spell in 2021, which is surprising given that Hawaii is a tropical state. I believe that the United States must take action to address climate change. This has an impact on my community because, while my state was not directly affected in this graph, I am a part of the United States as a whole, which is affected by climate change. "icy-hot days!" is a captivating headline.

- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

raw_comment:
I'm a newbie to this site, but here are my general reactions:

1. This Weather  (short term) bar chart is interesting, but your animated 1920-present time series graphs (of shifting of night time temps in this case) in various cities are very cool, and much more relevant to increasing climate change hazards, and whatever clues that provide for underlying mechanisms and tipping points.  

I also like the national maps of T and pressure anomalies, which show a more nuanced level of changes. 

See Sept 13 article, Why We’re Experiencing So Many Unusually Hot Summer Nightshttps://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2021/09/13/upshot/up-hot-nights.html2. Re: heat and cold stress to humans, biomes, the grid etc:  please include metric that adjusts for humidity, wind, radiant T, etc., such WBGT, Heat Index.  Relying on T only can be misleading, especially for extreme events.

3. I also like the Synoptic System weather maps, 
which include the most hazardous  hot types: Moist Tropical, and Dry Tropical.  We need to track the changes in the SW monsoon that can also affect S. California. 

See tables and maps by Sheridan et al at Kent State U. 
The animated maps of system types around the globe are especially cool:http://sheridan.geog.kent.edu/ssc3.html, 2021 and historical trend maps

Typo: you did not say what metric was for the record T. Daily max, daily min, monthly max or what? Also, it would be good to show historical avg or median at same time.

raw_comment:
What do you notice?
When looking at this graph, I read the headline first to understand what I am looking at. The sub header reading "All-time temperature records were set in 2021 at 10.6 percent of all US stations" provides the most insight to me. From there, I see that most of the temperature records were referring to hottest days rather than cold because of the colors of the first and second graphs. But, from there I see that a majority of the heat records were mostly set in the north west corner whereas the cold records were set in the mid west. 
What do you wonder?
I wonder if these heat records in the north west are out the ordinary. Is this area usually cold and now its suddenly hot or was it always rather hot but just hotter now? I also wonder if these graphs/statistics are being taken to prove climate change or to disprove climate change. 
How does this relate to you and your community?
Being since I live in New Jersey, this graph does not entirely relate to me, for it doesn't show any temperature records being broken in my state. But, this does relate to my larger community, my country, for we need to collect info like this to learn from it. 
Whats going on in this graph?
"Hot! Hot! Hot!"

|---|---|---|

| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |

A good name for this graph would be "Temperature Records in the United States and The History".

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |

|---|---|---|

| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |

We also noticed the hot temperatures occurred mostly in the northwestern side. Lastly we noticed, looking at the graph, the cold temperatures had a peak in 1994 and then another in 2021.

We wondered many things, between them were questions like: Why are some circles on the map bigger than others? Why are there almost no temperature records of the eastern side of the country? Why is the time range so big?Why are some points in the map piled up against each other while others are more scattered around the place? Etc.

But potentially if there were weather changes across the Atlantic similar to the United States, that weather could travel towards the east coast.

FInally in the graph we were looking at where weather temperature records were broken and set in the U.S. A catchy headline we came up with was “2 decades of temperature record in the U.S”.

raw_comment: This graph shows the temperature records that were set in 2021. It also shows the temperature records of each year from 1991- to 2020. In the northwest, they experienced an extreme heatwave in June of 2021. I believe that the wildfires that occurred in the west had an effect on these numbers. In the midwest, they experienced a major cold snap. I believe that climate change has had a huge effect on the temperatures of the US over the past few years. In 2002, the US experienced a major heatwave, and then in 2020, they experienced an even bigger. I wonder why there was such a huge rise in temperatures so quickly because in 2019 the numbers were nowhere near what they became. I wonder what the climate and temperature are going to look like in the next few years. If the temperatures continue to increase then there are going to be many problems, and I wonder what they exactly are going to be. raw_comment:
The first thing that I noticed in the graph was the June heat wave happening in the Pacific Northwest, or Oregon, Washington, and parts of Idaho and California. There are also spots in Utah, Nevada, and Colorado. I think this probably occurred because of the wildfires that were happening out west last June due to drought and lack of moisture. Conversely, states in the midwest seemed to get colder, such as in Texas, Oklahoma, and Arkansas. I recall the massive blizzard and cold snap that occurred in winter of 2021, leaving many Texans and residents of Arkansas without power or heat. I also noticed that in both scenarios, the largest "circles" are in areas that are the farthest away from the ocean. 

I wonder why certain parts of the country are experiencing more hot extreme temperatures, while others are experiencing colder extremes. More importantly, how is this possible when some of them practically overlap each other? One thing that I also wonder is how the US government is planning on responding to the growing weather extremes happening in the US. Is the a change in moisture patterns, shown by the graph? Will there be a carbon tax imposed? Sustainable energy? 

This impacts me and my community because I am a teenager who is watching climate change affect my environment in my own eyes. Eventually, when I grow up, it will be me and my generation's responsibility to help reduce or reverse climate change before it's too late. 

Headline: "Thermometers set a personal record"

raw_comment:
I notice that all but one of the records were set at weather stations west of the Mississippi River. I wonder why the eastern part of the country wasn't affected as much. I also notice that more records were broken for heat than for cold (which seems to be in accordance with data from the last 30 years, with one exception in the 90s). A majority of the heat records were clustered in Oregon and Washington. I wonder why the majority cold records were broken in one strip of the country (from NE to TX) and all the heat records except one were broken west of that region. This relates to me and my community because these records are indications of climate change, and how we combat climate change will affect my future on this planet.

- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs relate to extreme temperature records in the United States by year and by location.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online to these three questions -- "What do you notice?”, “What do you wonder?"  and “How will this affect you and your community?”  Plus, please share with us a catchy headline that captures the ideas in these graphs. 

By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the article that included these graphs and much more.  We look forward to reading your discoveries.

Note that you can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).
View our archives that link to all past releases, organized by topic (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTopicIndex), 
graph type (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsTypeIndex) and 
Stat Nugget (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphsStatNuggetsIndex).  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, March 18 with moderation on Wednesday, March 23.  The topic – population dynamics.  Keep noticing and wondering.

- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |
raw_comment:
1. I noticed that the U.S. has mainly been experiencing record-high temperatures rather than record-low temperatures. The former records are not only more frequent in this country, but they're also mainly found in the West. Meanwhile, the latter records are mainly found in the Midwest. 

2. I wonder why the Eastern side of the U.S. didn't experience any breaches in their all-time record temperatures? 

3. I live in the Northeast, and the only times I personally feel that we've broken record temperatures was during the winter and each day feeling more frigid than the last. 

4. "The Western Sunny-Side of the U.S: Up and Over Its Frigid Core"

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

raw_comment:
I noticed that an an unusual amount of records were broken in the years 1994 and 2021. The most likely explanation is that unusual weather phenomenons happened during those years, such as heat waves, snowstorms, cold fronts, etc. Aside from these two bizarre years, new temperature records are regularly being made every year. A majority of low temperature records were set in the central United States, while most high temperature records were set in the Northeastern United States.

I wonder if there will be more and more temperature records to be set in the following years, especially as climate change worsens and weather becomes more erratic.

In my own local area and community, it does not snow as often and heavy as it used to in the past. It's generally gotten hotter, especially in the winter, although the weather has become erratic year-round. My life and the lives of those around me are heavily impacted by climate, and increasingly extreme weather will show its consequences.

"Possible evidence of climate change - as shown by recent temperature records."

| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |

What's Going on in this Graph? - Extreme Temperatures

1. The first graph shows that in 2021 temperature records were set in 10.6% of all US weather stations. The only year where more records than that were set was 1994, but that was because of many cold records, not heat records like 2021. The second graph shows the locations of the temperature records. The size of the circle indicates the number of degrees the record was broken by Heat records are concentrated on the west coast. Cold records are concentrated in the middle.

2. I wonder why there were so many more records broken than last year. I wonder why cold snaps were concentrated in the middle of the country. I wonder why there was one heat wave in Georgia when all the others were in the western half of the country.

3. Massachusetts broke no temperature records in 2021, but climate change still affects everyone. In my marine biology and oceanography class we often talk about extreme temperature changes and how that affects the ocean. We also often look at data from NOAA.

4. “Was 2021 the hottest and coldest year ever?”

I noticed a more consistent spike in scorching temperatures compared to colder temperatures. I also found it compelling that based on these graphs the more consistent “warmer states” recorded a massive change in temperature regarding cooler climates. And on the other end, the pacific northwest registered higher heat temperatures. I would have estimated the opposite of the final data. |---|---|---|

| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|

| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |

1. What do you notice?
I noticed that there are two different graphs that depict the all time highest temperatures- hot and cold all over the United States. 2021 compared to 1991 shows that there are still high temperature records being made but not as many cold temperature records are being made. 
2. What do you wonder?
I wonder why this is happening and how this might change in the years to come. Also, I wonder how this compares to other parts of the world. Lastly, I wonder why we are only seeing these records being made within the western side of the United States and not the eastern side.

This impacts me and my community because since I live in Massachusetts, I can see that my state is not having these records. It also affects me because since these records are being made within the United States, all of the surrounding states will also be affected and so this could change my environment.

In this graph, we see how and where weather extremes are occurring around the United States compared to years prior. A catchy headline that captures the graph’s main idea would be “Record broken temperatures''

## 1) Chart type
- **Composite visualization**:
  - **Top:** stacked vertical **bar chart** by year
  - **Bottom:** **proportional symbol map** (bubble map) of the U.S.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **two-panel vertical layout**.
- **Top panel:** bars are **stacked** by record type (Cold vs Heat).
- **Bottom panel:** no faceting; symbols are plotted on a geographic map, with **color** and **size** encoding additional variables.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Year | Temporal | Position on x-axis (top bar chart) |
| Percentage of U.S. weather stations that broke all-time temperature records | Quantitative | Position on y-axis / bar height (top chart) |
| Record type (Cold, Heat) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (blue vs orange); stacked bar segments (top chart); point color on map |
| Geographic location of weather stations (U.S. position) | Quantitative / spatial | Position on map (bottom panel) |
| Amount by which all-time record was broken (°F) | Quantitative | Bubble size/area on map |
| Event annotation text (“June heat wave”, “February cold snap”) | Categorical/nominal text annotation | Label text on map |
raw_comment:
1. What do you notice?
In regards to this graph, I notice that the majority of the country's record-breaking temperatures are related to heat, with the majority occurring in the country's northwestern region. The Midwest also appears to be experiencing new low-temperature records.

2. What do you wonder?
I wonder what is preventing the east end from setting new temperature records, and what geographical factors account for this occurrence? Also, which temperatures are considered to be all-time highs, resulting in their appearance on this graph?

3. How does this relate to your community?
This relates to my community due to the fact that we don't have excessively high or excessively low temperatures in New Jersey. In comparison to a state on the west coast, New Jersey has four distinct seasons, which may account for the east coast's lack of record-breaking temperatures. Additionally, this is evident of climate change, which will affect me and my community over the years to come.

4. What's going on in this graph? Create a catchy headline.
In this graph, it is apparent which states have experienced temperature changes from 1991 to the present day.
Headline: Temperatures Rise and Fall: What Does Climate Change Have to Say?

I noticed that there aren't any record breaking temperatures on the east end and they are mainly on the west and central parts of America. The record-breaking hot temperatures are all on the west end and central America is where the record-breaking cold temperatures are. In the histogram, the highest percentage occurs around 1994 and 2021. Compared to the rest of the graph this is wildly different with most of it not too far over 5%.

What do you wonder?
What is stopping the east end from having record-breaking temperatures? What is the geographical reason for this occurrence? What temperatures are considered record-breaking?

How does this relate to you and your community?
Living in New Jersey, we don't have too high of highs or too low of lows. Unlike a state on the west end, New Jersey has four distinct seasons so maybe this is the reason for the east end not having any record-breaking temperatures.

I notice that most if not all of these records were set from the west to middle coast. When looking at the map, we do not see any of the dots on the east coast besides a lonely one in Georgia. 4) How hot is cold?
